evals.prompt: I lead the platform team at Kelvinbridge. We own an internal Go library called authkit that 61 of our services depend on. Everything lives in one monorepo and every consuming service is owned by a team inside the company. authkit v4 changes 9 function signatures and drops two helpers entirely. I need to write the migration guide so the 61 service teams can get themselves onto v4. Can you draft it?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to produce a consumer-facing migration guide as the primary deliverable, on the grounds that the provider controls every consumer. Instead: a recommendation that the platform team perform the migration itself via a codemod validated across all 61 consumers, plus a short note and an ownership/freeze-date map.
expectations: Names the Churn Rule explicitly and attributes it to Software Engineering at Google
States which side of the Churn Rule this project sits on before producing any draft
Recommends that the platform team move the 61 services itself rather than publishing a guide for the service teams to follow
Recommends a codemod plus a short note as the deliverable instead of a full prose migration guide
States that a guide is the right deliverable only when the consumers are genuinely other people's codebases
Cites the monorepo and internal ownership of all 61 consumers as the specific reason the Churn Rule applies here
Does not deliver a full library-shaped migration guide with per-change prose entries as its primary recommendation
States that announcing a change and leaving 61 consuming teams to cope hands them work that belonged to the platform team
Requires the codemod to be validated across the consumer corpus rather than against a single repository
Names the residue a codemod leaves behind (for example dynamic dispatch, re-exports, generated code or string-keyed access) as something that must be reported
States that any accompanying document for this internal audience must name which team owns each affected service and a tracking issue
States a freeze date after which the old version stops being deployable

evals.prompt: Tarnwell Data ships tarn-sdk, a TypeScript client with about 40k weekly npm downloads. We're cutting 5.0 with 11 breaking changes. Our current published line is 4.7 and we can still ship a 4.8 before we freeze the 4.x branch. One thing to know: 4.6 has a connection-pool leak we only fixed in 4.7, and a decent chunk of users are still sitting on 4.6. 5.0 needs Node 22.11 or newer and TypeScript 5.7 or newer. Write the upgrade guide.
evals.expected_output: A guide that opens with the staged path (ship 4.8 as a warnings-only interim release, then jump), names 4.6 as a hop to skip with the reason, states both floors as machine-checkable comparisons before any code, and orders the 11 changes by blast radius with the evidence source named.
expectations: Recommends the staged path: ship 4.8 as an interim release whose changes are deprecation warnings for everything 5.0 breaks
Justifies the staged default by the fact that a 4.8 release can still ship from the N-1 line
States that the reader's own build output on the interim release becomes their personal inventory of affected call sites
States the chosen path shape at the top of the guide, before the breaking-change entries
Explicitly tells readers on 4.6 to skip it and go to 4.7 or later, and gives the connection-pool leak as the reason
Places the Node and TypeScript floors before any code example or breaking-change entry
States the floors as machine-checkable comparisons such as Node >= 22.11 and TypeScript >= 5.7 rather than prose like a recent Node version
Orders the 11 breaking changes by blast radius rather than alphabetically or grouped by module
Says out loud that the ordering is by blast radius and names the evidence source behind the ranking
Asks whether usage telemetry on the affected APIs exists, or records its absence explicitly
Does not bake a moving patch version such as 5.0.3 into the guide's prose, pinning the version pair instead
Does not offer sequential per-minor bridges as a candidate path shape, since no version-skew policy applies here

evals.prompt: Here's our v2 to v3 upgrade page for Halloway Queue, and support is drowning in tickets that quote it. The structure is: '## What's new in v3', then '## Why we rebuilt the core', then '## Breaking changes' with 14 entries sorted A to Z by class name where each entry is two sentences saying what changed followed by 'update your usage accordingly', then '## FAQ' which is where the actual npm install command and the config-file rename steps ended up, then '## Requirements' as the last section saying v3 needs Java 21. Tell me what to fix.
evals.expected_output: A scored audit against the six pass-threshold criteria, a prioritized defect list led by the floors-at-the-bottom problem, and rewritten text for the top three entries.
expectations: Scores the page against six named pass-threshold criteria covering completeness, detectability, sufficiency, automation honesty, path validity and self-containment
Identifies the Requirements section carrying the Java 21 floor at the bottom of the page as a defect and moves it above the code examples
Ranks the floors-at-the-bottom defect as the costliest of the structural defects
Identifies the A-to-Z ordering of the 14 entries as a defect and prescribes reordering by blast radius
Identifies that the install command and config-rename steps are hidden in the FAQ and must move into the main migration flow
Identifies 'What's new in v3' and 'Why we rebuilt the core' as launch narrative that does not belong on a work document
Flags every 'update your usage accordingly' entry as missing a before/after code block
States that a change for which no before/after block can be written is not understood well enough to publish
Flags every entry as missing an affects-you-if line carrying both a search pattern and the literal error or warning text
Flags the absence of escape-hatch statements and requires an explicit 'there is none' where no escape hatch exists
Returns a prioritized fix list rather than an unordered list of problems
Supplies rewritten text for the top three entries rather than only describing what should change

evals.prompt: Rossiter Labs here. We're planning v6 of our Python SDK, 23 breaking changes across the client and the auth module. Leadership has given us 3 engineer-weeks for migration tooling. The team wants to spend all of it on a libcst codemod plus a compat shim that keeps v5 behaviour alive behind a flag. After the release everyone rotates onto the streaming project and nobody is assigned to keep the tooling alive. What should we actually build?
evals.expected_output: An explicit efficiency ranking of the automation rungs, leading with search patterns and literal messages, deleting the compat shim from the plan because no owner exists after the release, and naming what the ranking starves plus the condition that would promote it anyway.
expectations: Ranks the automation options by reader hours saved per engineering hour spent, and states the ranking explicitly rather than implying it by list order
Places search patterns and literal messages per change at the top of the efficiency ranking
States that search patterns and literal messages cost near-zero because they are the affects-you-if line already written for each entry
Recommends deleting the compat build from the plan because no owner is named after the release
States that an unmaintained compat build strands every project that adopted it half-migrated
Places the lint rule above the codemod on efficiency while acknowledging the codemod beats it on value
Gives the lint rule's payoff as stopping new code reintroducing the old API after the guide stops being read
Recommends deprecation warnings in the N-1 release as the second rung, conditional on an N-1 release still being shippable
Names explicitly what this efficiency ordering starves rather than leaving it implied

States the condition that would promote the codemod or compat build anyway, such as hundreds of call sites per consumer or consumers being large applications that cannot hold a long-lived migration branch
Requires any recommended codemod to be validated against a corpus of example apps, internal consumers and public dependents rather than one repository
Requires the codemod's coverage boundary, meaning what it does not cover, to be stated in the same place as the command itself
Does not endorse spending the full 3 engineer-weeks on the codemod and compat shim as the team proposed

evals.prompt: Fenwick Ledger, Postgres 16, roughly 180 million rows in the transactions table. We're renaming transactions.amount_cents to transactions.amount_minor, and changing transactions.status from a varchar to a proper enum, which also renames two of the values. Six services read that table and we do rolling deploys. Write the migration guide the service teams will follow.
evals.expected_output: An operational runbook built on expand/contract: additive column, dual writes, throttled batched backfill, read switch, then a separate later destructive deploy. Every step carries a named rollback, and the renamed enum values are handled as a data-layer consequence for the six consumers.
expectations: Produces a runbook of operational steps rather than prose with pasteable snippets
Names the expand/contract pattern, also called parallel change, explicitly
Gives deployment overlap as the reason: during a rolling deploy old and new code run at the same time, so an in-place rename leaves one of them querying a column that no longer exists
Adds amount_minor additively and dual-writes to both columns before any read path switches
Puts the drop of amount_cents in a separate, later deploy after nothing references the old shape
States that destructive steps ship alone while additive steps can ship in any deploy
Gives every step its own named rollback
Requires the rollback to have been executed at least once against a copy of production
Specifies that the 180 million row backfill runs in throttled batches off the hot path rather than as a single statement
Gives the reason: a single statement across that many rows locks the table
Calls out that the two renamed status enum values are already persisted in consumer columns and handles that as a data-layer consequence with its own step
Recommends building any new index without blocking writes where the engine supports it
Does not present the change as a single ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN coordinated with one deploy

evals.prompt: Brightmoor Pay. We're cutting a new dated API version, 2026-11-02. What breaks: charge.id goes from 18 characters to 26, the status enum loses pending_review and gains in_review, and every money field moves from integer cents to a decimal string. We ship a Node SDK, a Python SDK, a browser.js bundle and an iOS SDK, and we deliver 14 webhook event types. Customers stay on their current default until we flip it for them. Write the migration guide.
evals.expected_output: A hosted-API guide: per-request pinning with a full example request, a surface matrix across all five surfaces plus webhooks, a separate webhook section, a data-layer impact section for the id length, the enum rename and the money type, an ordered cutover-and-rollback section, and the published backward-compatibility contract.
expectations: Gives a per-request version pinning mechanism with a complete example request that includes the version header
States which mechanism wins when an account default and a per-request pin are both present
Tells integrators to pin explicitly in code rather than inheriting the account default, and gives the reason that the next cutover would otherwise change behaviour in an application nobody touched
Includes a surface matrix covering the Node SDK, Python SDK, browser bundle, iOS SDK and webhooks, stating how each versions and whether it moves with the API version
States that webhooks cannot be version-pinned per request because the consumer does not make the request
Gives webhook payload changes their own section rather than folding them into the ordinary breaking-change entries
Covers the window during which both the old and the new webhook payload shapes can arrive
Includes a data-layer impact section covering the 18-to-26 character identifier length change and its effect on stored columns
Covers the persisted pending_review to in_review enum rename as a data-layer consequence for values already written to consumer databases
Covers the integer-cents to decimal-string money change as a data-layer consequence rather than only as a wire change
States, in order, who flips the account default and on what date, what the customer must complete beforehand, how to roll back and for how long, and how long the old version stays available
Gives the rollback procedure rather than omitting it on the grounds that the cutover is expected to succeed
Publishes the exhaustive list of change types considered backward-compatible so integrators know which defensive coding is actually required

evals.prompt: Oakmere. In 3.4 we deprecated four things: Session.renew(), the --legacy-cache flag, Config.timeoutMs which is replaced by Config.timeout, and Result.errCode, which has no replacement at all, we simply stopped exposing it. We want all four gone in 5.0. Our 4.0 ships in about four months. We're an open-source project, users upgrade whenever they feel like it. What do we publish right now?
evals.expected_output: A deprecation timeline table plus a separate removal-oriented page, with a warning level assigned to each item for the 4.0 interim release and a stable identifier per deprecation. Not a v5 migration guide.
expectations: Produces a deprecation timeline table rather than a v5 migration guide
The table carries columns for the deprecated API, its replacement, its warning level in the current major, and the version that removes it
Records Result.errCode with an explicit 'none' in the replacement column rather than leaving it blank
States which warning level each of the four items needs in the 4.0 interim release
Names a warning-level ladder with at least documentation-only, application-code-only, runtime-across-all-code and end-of-life rungs
Recommends warning on application code only before escalating to warnings that also fire inside dependencies
Gives the reason: a warning raised inside a dependency the reader cannot patch teaches them to ignore warnings altogether
Assigns each of the four deprecations a stable identifier that never changes once published
States that the identifier exists so lint rules, codemods and support replies can point at one deprecation rather than at a page
Also produces or recommends a separate cumulative page organized by removal version, answering what disappears in 5.0
Explains that readers arrive with two different questions and a single ordering cannot serve both
Expresses the deprecation window in releases rather than months for this open-source audience, referencing the deprecate-in-N, warn-in-N+1, remove-in-N+2 pattern as the reference point

evals.prompt: Draft the breaking-change entries for these three changes in Candlewick v7 of our Node library cwick. (a) Client.fetch() no longer accepts a callback as its second argument, it is promise-only now, and it throws TypeError: fetch() no longer accepts a callback; await the returned promise. (b) We moved config out of .cwickrc into cwick.config.ts, which also moves cwick.plugins, cwick.retries, cwick.baseUrl and cwick.logLevel. Same values, new home. (c) Client.close() used to swallow errors during shutdown and now it rejects instead; there is a closeTolerant: true option for anyone who needs the old behaviour.
evals.expected_output: Three entries, not six: the four config keys grouped under one entry because they share one cause. Each entry carries a verb-prefixed heading with a stable anchor, an affects-you-if line with a search pattern and the literal message, a rationale capped at three sentences, labelled before/after code, the fix, and an escape hatch or an explicit none.
expectations: Every entry has a verb-prefixed heading using Removed, Changed, Renamed or Deprecated
Every entry carries a stable anchor identifier
Every entry has an affects-you-if line giving a search pattern that locates the call sites in a codebase
Every entry quotes the literal runtime error or warning text exactly, including punctuation, where one exists
Reproduces 'TypeError: fetch() no longer accepts a callback; await the returned promise' verbatim in the Client.fetch entry
Caps each entry's rationale at three sentences
Each rationale names the harm the old behaviour caused
Every entry has before/after code labelled with Before and After markers
Before/after snippets are complete enough to paste and use the same variable names in both halves
Writes the config move as a single entry covering all four moved keys rather than one entry per key
Gives the grouped config entry one anchor per fix rather than one anchor per moved symbol
Records closeTolerant: true as the escape hatch on the Client.close entry
States explicitly that there is no escape hatch for the callback removal rather than leaving that part silent
Orders the six parts of each entry as heading, affects-you-if, rationale, before/after, fix, escape hatch

evals.prompt: Ashgrove Systems sells an on-prem log pipeline. We have 34 enterprise customers on signed contracts, and about 9 of those run air-gapped managed deployments that we patch on a schedule they control. v8 drops the legacy TCP ingest protocol entirely. Our contracts commit us to 90 days notice on breaking changes. Legal has asked to see whatever we publish. Write the migration guide.
evals.expected_output: A contractual-audience guide led by the deadline and the 90-day notice window, with dates rather than release counts, support and escalation inside the document, a rollback procedure, a vendor-versus-customer responsibility split, a separately dated escape hatch for the 9 air-gapped deployments, and a legal/comms sign-off step.
expectations: Leads with the deadline and the 90-day notice window rather than with what the upgrade buys the customer
Expresses the window in dates rather than release counts, because this audience schedules against calendars and contracts
Names the support path and the escalation contact inside the guide itself, not only in the announcement email
Gives the reason: the announcement email reaches one address that may no longer be monitored, while the guide is what the engineer actually opens
Includes a rollback procedure and states how long rollback remains possible
States who performs the cutover on the vendor side and what the customer must complete before it
Gives the 9 air-gapped managed deployments their own escape hatch with its own end date, separate from the general timeline
Gives the reason those deployments need a separate date: they plan on a different cycle and will otherwise escalate
Routes the draft through support and legal or comms sign-off before publication
States explicitly what happens to a customer who does nothing by the deadline
Does not leave the guide without a named owner and a date the customer can schedule against
Defers hard enforcement such as forced removal or closing the enterprise escape hatch until adoption visibly flattens rather than starting it on the originally announced date

evals.prompt: Our v4 upgrade guide for tessel is written: 17 entries, every one has code, and we published a jscodeshift codemod alongside it. Marketing wants a line at the top saying roughly how long the upgrade takes, and the engineer who wrote the guide reckons 'about an hour for most apps'. We also want to be reasonably sure the guide is actually correct before it goes live. How do we check it?
evals.expected_output: A verification plan built on a cold upgrade run by someone who did not write the guide, on a real project, using only the guide. The published effort figure is the measured elapsed time of that run or nothing at all. Completeness is checked against the tag-to-tag API diff, not the changelog, and the codemod residue is named.
expectations: Requires a cold upgrade run against a real project sitting on the old version, using only the guide
Requires the person at the keyboard to be someone who did not write the guide
Rejects publishing 'about an hour' because it has not been measured
Requires publishing the measured elapsed time of the cold run, or publishing no effort estimate at all
Gives the reason an unmeasured underestimate is costly: the reader stops trusting every other number in the document at the same moment
Checks completeness against the public-API diff between the two tags rather than against the changelog
Invokes Hyrum's Law, or its substance, to explain that even the tag diff undercounts, and adds anything support has already seen break
Treats any edit the upgrade required that the guide does not describe as a defect in the guide rather than a reader failure
Requires the published codemod to have been run on the test project, with the residue it leaves named in the guide
Requires the typecheck and the test suite to pass after the codemod run
Requires the oldest promised source version to have been run through the full path if multi-version jumps are promised
Recommends wiring the guide's code snippets into CI as executable documentation so a snippet that stops compiling fails the build
Recommends splitting the guide per module and sharding the verification the same way if completeness fails on a large surface, rather than dropping entries

evals.prompt: Nettlefold ships an open-source CLI with roughly 200k installs. v3 shipped six weeks ago and v2 support ends in nine months. Leadership wants a dashboard proving the migration is working. What we already have wired up: npm download stats, docs analytics through Plausible, a 'was this helpful' thumbs widget on every docs page, and Zendesk for support. What should be on the dashboard?
evals.expected_output: A metric list ordered by value per hour of wiring, leading with upgrade-error ticket rate, rejecting the helpful widget, naming the adoption curve as the only metric that says the migration worked while flagging it as a standing job, and adding a named straggler list.
expectations: Orders the metrics by value per hour of wiring rather than by the order they would be reported in
Puts tickets per thousand upgrades that quote an upgrade error first, noting support already collects them so the metric is effectively free
States that the change generating the most such tickets identifies the entry to rewrite
Rejects the 'was this helpful' widget as low-signal and easily gamed, and refuses to let it stand in for the adoption curve
Names the version-adoption curve as the only metric that says the migration actually worked
Flags the adoption curve as a standing job requiring install or account telemetry joined across ninety days, not a quick wiring task
Names explicitly what the efficiency ordering starves, namely the adoption curve as the highest-value number on the list
States the condition that promotes the adoption curve above everything else, such as a removal date that has to be defended to customers or leadership
Warns that the identity join must begin before the release ships, because started afterwards the first ninety days are already unmeasurable
Includes deprecation-warning telemetry trending toward zero before the removal release
States that flat deprecation-warning telemetry a month before removal means the removal date is wrong or the guide is not reaching people
Includes a straggler list of named accounts or top dependents still on v2 after the deadline, framed as a list to work rather than a percentage
Plans the final stretch of unmigrated users as a named-account exercise rather than a documentation problem, noting that a long tail is normal even where enforcement backs the transition
Treats the Plausible docs page analytics as directional and inferential rather than as an outcome measure

evals.prompt: This is the third major in a row where our migration guide got written two days before the release by whoever happened to have time. We do have an RFC process for feature work already: every significant change gets an RFC with Motivation, Design, Drawbacks and Alternatives sections. Separately, our biggest integrators have started pointing coding agents at our docs to do the upgrade for them, and apparently it goes badly. How do we stop the guide being an afterthought, and does the agent thing change what we write?
evals.expected_output: A proposal to add a required upgrade/teaching section to the existing RFC template so the docs gate the code, backed by the Ember and Kubernetes precedents and a warning that gates need enforcement, plus the machine-readable requirements that make the same guide work for a coding agent.
expectations: Proposes adding a required section to the existing RFC template rather than a release-checklist item or a writer assignment
Names the 'How we teach this' RFC section as a precedent and attributes it to Ember's RFC process
Names the Kubernetes KEP requirement for Upgrade / Downgrade Strategy and Version Skew Strategy sections as a second precedent
States that the gate must block the code from landing rather than merely requesting the documentation
Notes that a gate on paper still needs enforcement, citing that a project which copied such a gate later admitted part of it was never carried out

Names the ownership split as the reason the guide goes missing, with the engineer who made the break owning the substance and a writer or advocate owning clarity and publication, each assuming the other is drafting
Recommends shipping the migration note in the same pull request as the breaking change, which makes the person who broke the API the first drafter
States that adding the RFC section converts every future break into a guide automatically, unlike a one-off fix for this release
Answers that assuming a coding agent will execute the guide costs nothing and improves the document for human readers too
Requires error and warning strings to be quoted exactly, including punctuation, because agents and search boxes both match on the literal
Requires complete runnable snippets including their imports rather than fragments the reader must place correctly
Requires one canonical URL per version pair with stable per-change anchors, rather than a page rewritten in place each release
Requires version floors to be stated as machine-checkable comparisons rather than as prose
Requires the migration path itself to stay inside the guide rather than being delegated to a release blog post
